content: Methyl violet refers to a group of chemically related compounds that are primarily used as pH indicators and dyes. These compounds are mixtures of tetramethyl, pentamethyl, and hexamethyl pararosanilins. By varying the proportions of these components, manufacturers can produce different shades of violet in the final dye. The degree of methylation (the number of methyl groups attached to the compound) determines the depth of the blue color in the dye. Tetramethyl pararosanilin, also known as methyl violet 2B, is a specific chemical used in both chemistry and medicine. Pentamethyl pararosanilin, referred to as methyl violet 6B, is darker in color compared to 2B when used as a dye. Hexamethyl pararosanilin, known as methyl violet 10B or crystal violet, is even darker than 2B and often darker than 6B. In its pure form, tetramethyl pararosanilin appears as lustrous blue-green crystals with a melting point of 137°C (279°F). The primary application of methyl violet, in terms of global usage, is as a dye for textiles, where it imparts a purple or deep violet color. It is also used in paints and printing inks. As a pH indicator, methyl violet changes color depending on the pH of the solution: it turns yellow in acidic conditions and bluish-violet in alkaline conditions. It can be supplied as pre-made pH testing paper or as pure crystals that are dissolved in the sample being tested. In medicine, methyl violet 10B is commonly known as gentian violet. It is the active ingredient in Gram's stain, a critical tool for bacterial classification. Gentian violet has cytotoxic properties, meaning it destroys cells, and is used as a moderate-strength external disinfectant. However, it is highly toxic to most animals, including dogs and cats, and should never be applied to their skin as a disinfectant. Methyl violet also has the ability to bind to DNA, which makes it useful in biomedical sciences for cell viability assays. However, this DNA-binding property can interfere with DNA replication, potentially causing mutations and increasing the risk of cancer. Methyl violets are soluble in water, ethanol, diethylene glycol, and dipropylene glycol, with a solubility of 21% in ethanol. It is important to note that methyl violet should not be confused with methyl blue or methylene blue, which are distinct staining agents.
